definition: In this historical context, "cogito ergo sum" names Descartes’ claim that the act of thinking establishes the thinker’s existence. The source presents it as an early philosophical expression of mental unity, later paralleled by Kant’s idea of a unifying "I think."

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Mental Unity; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not state (or summarize) that “cogito ergo sum” names Descartes’ claim that thinking establishes the thinker’s existence; it only mentions Descartes’ phrase in connection with Kant’s “ich denke” and the “transcendental unity of apperception.”

The packet mentions “Des cartes' ‘cogito ergo sum’ is followed by Kant's ‘ich denke,’ a principle of the ‘transcendental unity of apperception,’” but it does not explicitly frame this as a “later paralleled” unifying “I think” claim in the way the definition describes.

The packet links Descartes’ “cogito ergo sum” to Kant’s “ich denke” and the “transcendental unity of apperception,” but it does not support the gloss that the phrase means the act of thinking establishes the thinker’s existence.
The definition adds an interpretive claim about “early philosophical expression of mental unity” that is broader than the packet’s wording and not directly stated there.
